Title: AKUH's 'Signs, Symptoms and Care' programme cancer is the second highest cause of death in children upto fourteen
NewsSubTitle: AKUH acquires latest radiation treatment facility to offer comprehensive cancer care
NewsSummary: Aga Khan University Hospital has added a state-of-the-art radiation treatment (Radiotherapy) facility to its existing cancer care services and now offers a fully comprehensive cancer care programme to patients.
NewsContent:
Aga Khan University Hospital has added a state-of-the-art radiation treatment (Radiotherapy) facility to its existing cancer care services and now offers a fully comprehensive cancer care programme to patients. This was stated by AKUH's Chief Radiation Oncologist, Dr Farrok Karsan, at a public health awareness programme in Karachi. He was addressing AKU's 'Sign, Symptoms and Care' public health awareness programme held at AKUH auditorium on April 1, 2006.

The University Hospital has been providing surgery and systemic chemotherapy services to cancer patients. With the advent of radiotherapy, a fully comprehensive cancer care programme is being offered. All cancer clinics are now moved to Ibn Zuhr Building.

Explaining the process of Radiation Oncology, Dr Karsan informed the audience that Radiation Oncology is the treatment of (malignant) tumours with high energy x-rays.  It can be used as a standalone treatment or in combination with other modalities such as chemotherapy and/or surgery.

Dr Karsan said that the experience of having radiation treatments is very similar to that of having x-ray imaging of your body. The side effects however are limited to the area of the body that is being treated. The team of the Radiation Oncology department is well experienced to deal with the side effects, he said.

Dr. Zehra Fadoo, Consultant Paediatrician at AKUH, addressed the programme on the topic of 'Cancer in children - a curable disease'. She disclosed that there is high incidence of cancer in children living in the developing world, and "84% of the 166,000 children who are diagnosed with the disease worldwide live in developing countries," she said.

Dr Fadoo said that cancer is the second highest cause of death in children between the ages one to fourteen even though childhood cancer is comparatively rare. She said that significant advances have been made in diagnosis and therapy during the past four decades and the good news is that childhood cancer can largely be cured if detected sufficiently early. "Childhood cancer is twice as curable as adult cancer," she stated. Yet the children with cancer who live in the developing countries have less than 50% survival rate, as opposed to more than 80% in the developed world, she pointed out.

Dr Fadoo emphasised upon the importance of early detection, increasing awareness and access to most basic cancer treatments which would save lives of thousands children with cancer and make medical professionals' fight with cancer a success story.

Cancers in children are often difficult to recognise. Dr Fadoo pointed out that parents should be alert to any unusual sign or symptoms that persist. These include an unusual mass or swelling; unexplained fever for more than two weeks, a persistent localized pain; unexplained paleness and loss of energy; sudden tendency to bruise; frequent headaches associated with vomiting; eye or vision changes and excessive rapid weight loss. Early detection and proper referral is the key to success in the treatment of cancer.

As part of its outreach programme and societal commitment to create awareness of early diagnosis and timely treatment, AKUH has organised over 200 'Signs, Symptoms and Care' programmes in Karachi, Hyderabad and the UAE, benefiting more than 40,000 people. Similarly, Aga Khan University Hospital's Patient Welfare Programme offers financial assistance to those patients who are unable to afford the medical cost of treatment. In 2004, 74 per cent of all patients treated at AKUH were from low- to middle-income groups. Since the inception of this welfare programme in 1986, over Rs 1.4 billion has been disbursed to more than 250,000 needy patients.
